title: Amazon rigged $20bn worth of ads, US FTC lawsuit alleges
description: Amazon secretly overcharged more than a million advertising customers by manipulating online auctions it uses to set ad prices, according to a lawsuit
body: Amazon secretly overcharged more than a million advertising customers by manipulating online auctions it uses to set ad prices, according to a lawsuit filed by the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and a bipartisan group of 22 states.According to the lawsuit, filed on Monday, the alleged scheme has likely netted the firm $20bn (£14.8bn) from advertising customers since 2019."Amazon overrides and replaces the actual auction results with higher prices set by Amazon to increase its profits," says a complaint filed in the company's home state of Washington.In a statement to the BBC, Amazon said it "strongly disagrees" with the premise that it misled advertisers and called the suit "misguided."In addition to advertisers, the FTC, a US consumer watchdog, and the states say Amazon customers have also been harmed as extra costs are passed onto shoppers."Consumers are suffering, have suffered, and will continue to suffer substantial injury as a result," the complaint states, prompting swift pushback from Amazon."The FTC wants the public to believe this case is about higher prices for consumers. It is not," Amazon said in its statement.The company's shares fell following the announcement of the lawsuit, closing 2.5% lower on Monday.Many brands and sellers compete on Amazon to place Sponsored Product ads and Sponsored Brands ads when consumer search for products using keywords on Amazon's e-commerce platform.Those placements are then auctioned off to the highest bidder.The complaint accuses Amazon of secretly charging advertisers more in so-called "second price" auctions, whereby prospective advertisers expect to pay one cent more than the next highest bidder for each bid they win.But in practice, the complaint alleges, Amazon has charged its Sponsored Products advertisers their own winning bid close to 80% of the time.The lawsuit states that Amazon's methods were spurred because "it was unhappy about how much revenue its advertising auctions were generating". Amazon responded by saying the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate". "Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," Amazon said in its statement."Average winning bids fell 50% from 2019 to 2025 on Sponsored Products search ads, and roughly 92% of placed ads are not given to the highest bid," the company added.Amazon has tangled with the consumer watchdog in the past.Last year, it settled a case with the FTC that alleged that it enrolled millions of consumers in its Prime subscription offering without their consent, and knowingly made it difficult for consumers to cancel.Amazon settled the case for $2.5bn, including civil penalties and consumer refunds.

schema.headline: Amazon rigged $20bn worth of ads, US FTC lawsuit alleges

title: South Korea: Police officer admits to closing missing person cases on Jeju to avoid work
description: A South Korean police officer has admitted to closing missing persons cases without investigating them in order to avoid additional work, according to
body: A South Korean police officer has admitted to closing missing persons cases without investigating them in order to avoid additional work, according to authorities.The officer, surnamed Bu, was arrested earlier this month after he was accused of prematurely closing cases on the popular holiday island Jeju and lying to missing persons' families.Amid mounting public criticism, police embarked on belated searches for several missing persons on the island, and have since discovered four bodies in recent weeks.The scandal has prompted President Lee Jae Myung to vow to reform the police, as the government prepares to give the police more powers.On Tuesday, the Jeju Provincial Police said Bu had falsely closed at least two high-profile cases and had been charged with forgery of public electronic records, obstruction of official duties and dereliction of duty.In both cases, Bu had falsely claimed he had contacted the missing persons and then prematurely closed their cases without confirming their whereabouts and safety.A police statement said that during their investigations into Bu, he had "stated to the effect that 'the missing person was a typical adult so I thought about it carelessly. If the case was not closed, there would have been a lot to take care of, and out of a sense of pressure over the case handover, I falsely closed it'."One of the cases involved a 37-year-old woman named Jang Mi-ran who went missing in May and was reported missing by her boyfriend. At the time, Bu had told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to her and she did not want to meet the police nor be contacted by her boyfriend. Authorities later said that this was a complete fabrication by Bu.Bu had entered this false information into the system, and also logged that Jang had died in a traffic accident, before closing the case, according to authorities.Jang's body was found near a palm tree plantation on Jeju last week.In another case where a man in his 60s was reported missing in July, Bu similarly falsely claimed that he had spoken to the man and that the man did not want to be contacted.The man was eventually found dead earlier this month.Police also said that they believe Bu could have prematurely closed another 25 missing persons cases, though in some of those cases the people were eventually confirmed to be alive and safe.Violent crime is rare in South Korea, where suicide rates are among the highest in the world.While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month.This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for the country's police.The government had recently passed laws to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics.However, this move has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence.President Lee has vowed to reform the police in the wake of recent criticism.On Tuesday President Lee said that it was "regrettable" that because of a few "loach-like figures who muddy the well water", "the honour and pride of the majority of diligent police officers are being damaged".

schema.headline: South Korea: Police officer admits to closing missing person cases on Jeju to avoid work

title: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review
description: Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spe
body: Donald Trump has said the United States' position on the Falkland Islands is "one of many" under review, as he pressed the UK to increase military spending.The US president said the UK has "got some problems, but they'll get solved" when asked about defence funding as a follow-up question to his response on the Falklands.It comes after The Daily Telegraph reported, external US defence officials were drawing up proposals to incentivise Nato allies to meet their spending pledges, with a threat to oppose UK sovereignty over the Falklands among the possible options.The UK government responded by saying Falkland islanders "are British with a right to determine their own future".A spokesperson added: "The islanders have repeatedly expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory and our commitment to them is unwavering."The Falkland Islands, in the south-west Atlantic Ocean, remain the subject of a sovereignty dispute between Britain and Argentina. The two countries waged a brief but bitter war over the territory in 1982. A British military task force ejected Argentine forces, which had landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim.The 74-day conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine soldiers.Previous US administrations have formally recognised the UK's de facto administration of the islands, but have not taken a formal position regarding sovereignty.Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump was asked by the BBC if he was reviewing the US position on the Falkland Islands.The president replied: "I always review every position. That's just one of many."In April, an internal Pentagon email reported by Reuters suggested the US was considering options to punish Nato allies it believed had failed to support its war in Iran.The options reportedly included the prospect of the US reviewing its position on Britain's claim to the Falklands.

schema.headline: Trump says US position on Falklands 'one of many' under review

title: Times Square stabbing: Woman killed and suspect shot dead by police
description: A 32-year-old woman has been killed and another victim is in hospital following a double stabbing in Times Square, New York late on Monday afternoon.T
body: A 32-year-old woman has been killed and another victim is in hospital following a double stabbing in Times Square, New York late on Monday afternoon.The suspect, a woman wielding two knives, was shot by police. All three people were taken to hospital, where the female victim and the suspect were later pronounced dead, Mayor Zohran Mamdani told a news conference. The deceased victim was later identified as Erin Piacenti, a Bank of America employee. The male victim remains in a stable condition.New York Police Department (NYPD) Commissioner Jessica Tisch described the attack as "unprovoked" and said the stabbings took place 20 seconds apart.Citing preliminary information, Tisch said the NYPD call centre received several 911 calls at approximately 16:24 local time (21:00 BST) reporting a woman armed with two knives was stabbing people along Seventh Avenue in Times Square.Police believe the incident began near West 41st Street and Seventh Ave, in Midtown Manhattan.The suspect approached a man who had just exited the subway and was standing with his wife waiting to cross the street, Tisch told a news conference."A witness at the scene told investigators that he observed the subject remove two knives from a red Target bag before approaching the first victim. "The subject waved the knives before stabbing a 68-year-old man in the right side of his abdomen, in what appears to be a random and unprovoked attack." The 68-year-old was taken to Bellevue Hospital and is now stable.The suspect continued up Seventh Avenue towards 42nd Street, which is where she stabbed the second victim, Piacenti, who did not survive after being taken to hospital.Bank of America said in a statement to the BBC: "We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague. She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed. Our hearts go out to her family and all of her loved ones."The suspect continued on Seventh Avenue, which is when police tried to get her to drop her weapons, speaking to her for four minutes, the NYPD commissioner said."During the encounter she told the officers 'I'm not dropping anything, I'd rather kill both of you'. She repeated 'I will kill you'," Tisch said. The suspect waved knives towards the officers, who then used Tasers, which were "ineffective" and did not stop her from heading towards them.NYPD officers then shot the woman, who was later also pronounced dead at Bellevue Hospital.The suspect was later identified as 49-year-old Pamela Cisneros of Queens, New York City. She had never previously been arrested but had a "documented mental health history with the NYPD, with one incident in 2018 and one in 2019", Tisch added.A tourist from Boston, Melinda Puzon, told the BBC's US reporting partner CBS News that she heard the shots and saw "so many people on the street"."It's very shocking."Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that the incident happened on Monday after a previous version said it was on Wednesday

schema.headline: Times Square stabbing: Woman killed and suspect shot dead by police

title: Ex-congressman George Santos banned from betting platform Kalshi  for life
description: Prediction-market operator Kalshi has permanently barred former US congressman George Santos from trading on its platform.The company alleged that San
body: Prediction-market operator Kalshi has permanently barred former US congressman George Santos from trading on its platform.The company alleged that Santos, who was expelled from Congress following a series of fraud and identity-theft charges, placed bets in February related to his own attendance at US President Donald Trump's State of the Union address, according to a notice of disciplinary action.Kalshi said its compliance team concluded his activity showed signs of insider dealing, prompting the lifetime ban. It said it was acting independently without waiting for external enforcement action.Santos on X thanked Kalshi for the ban and said "Let's see how much longer you guys are around for".The BBC has contacted Santos for comment. In 2025, Trump ordered the release of Santos, who had been sentenced to a seven-year prison term for wire fraud and identity theft. He had served three months.In July, Santos agreed to pay $35,000 to settle a federal investigation by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission into his State of the Union trades.Kalshi, alleging Santos used non-public information to place bets, issued a penalty of $71,356 (£38,000).The disciplinary moves come at a moment when prediction markets – which allow users to wager on outcomes ranging from elections to economic indicators – are facing heightened scrutiny.Both Kalshi and rival Polymarket have reported an uptick in unusual trading patterns, forcing platforms to strengthen monitoring systems and respond more aggressively to potential misconduct.Kalshi said Santos's case was referred to federal authorities earlier this summer after internal systems flagged suspicious behaviour linked to his account.The company said the case centered on his trades in a market tied to whether he would attend Trump's address – an event he could directly influence.Its compliance team found he placed a series of sizeable bets between 2 and 25 February, some of which were based on false or misleading public statements about his plans, according to the company.His comments moved contract prices, and he ultimately earned $17,839.57 from the trades.Santos has denied wrongdoing in various matters but has admitted to stealing identities of nearly a dozen people, including next of kin. He pleaded guilty to wire fraud and aggravated identity theft and served three months in prison before Trump commuted his sentence last year.He embellished much about his biography in the run-up to his election to Congress in 2022. The former lawmaker was only the sixth in US history to be expelled from Congress.The Kalshi episode underscores the growing compliance burden facing prediction markets as they attract more users and move closer to mainstream products. Regulators have signalled that platforms will be expected to meet higher standards as the industry matures, particularly when political or economic events are involved.

schema.headline: Ex-congressman George Santos banned from betting platform Kalshi  for life

title: Festival honouring Dolly Parton set for Nashville and London
description: Dolly Parton's estate has announced a festival honouring the life and legacy of the late singer, set for London and Nashville.The "star-studded" two-d
body: Dolly Parton's estate has announced a festival honouring the life and legacy of the late singer, set for London and Nashville.The "star-studded" two-day DollyFest will happen across two consecutive weekends in both cities in 2027, her estate said in a Monday press release, adding that the specific dates will be announced later. Parton herself dreamed up an earlier version of the event, where she would host and perform alongside other artists, but the original January 2026 event was called off before it was announced publicly, due to Parton's health struggles, her estate said.  "DOLLYFEST will be the party of a lifetime she wanted to share with the world," her estate said.DollyFest will take the place of a traditional public memorial for the artist, who died at the age of 80 on 25 August after a brief battle with cancer.She was laid to rest at a private family funeral in Nashville on Friday, and placed next to her late husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in the Tennessee city, her great-niece said. DollyFest organiser Danny Nozell, the founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said the estate is not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in whatever ways they choose, but Parton did not want a traditional memorial. "It feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly," Nozell said. "This is something that is authentic to her, something that feels right to me, and something that artists and fans around the world can participate in, while also giving everyone time to grieve, and giving everyone time to plan."Originally from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, Parton was a country music icon, philanthropist and businesswoman whose most famous songs included Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You.In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote thousands of songs.Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."Since her death, emotional tributes from celebrities, politicians, and countless fans have flooded social media."A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DOLLYFEST is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!)," Nozell said.

schema.headline: Festival honouring Dolly Parton set for Nashville and London

title: US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case
description: Figure caption, Watch: New lawyer for D4vd could take "additional time" to proceed, says district attorneyBySareen Habeshian and Nardine SaadReporting
body: Figure caption, Watch: New lawyer for D4vd could take "additional time" to proceed, says district attorneyBySareen Habeshian and Nardine SaadReporting fromLos AngelesThe celebrity lawyers hired to represent US musician D4vd in his upcoming murder trial have withdrawn from the case.The star, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke, has been appointed a public defender to mount his defence against the charge of murdering Celeste Rivas Hernandez, 14, whose remains were found in September 2025 in a Tesla registered to his address.Burke, 21, pleaded not guilty to the murder charges in a Los Angeles court on Monday. A judge determined last month that he will stand trial for murder. Prosecutors have alleged he stabbed the teen after years of sexual abuse before dismembering her body.Image source, Getty ImagesA pre-trial hearing is set for 19 October. Lawyers Blair Berk, Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter said in a statement to the BBC that the court had granted their request to withdraw from the case and had appointed the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office to represent the singer. The statement said that D4vd "qualified for appointed counsel"."We continue to support David and his defence against these serious charges," they said. "We are grateful that the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office has taken over the representation and that David has a highly capable and committed team of attorneys and investigators behind him."Berk, who led the defence team, has previously represented US actor Mel Gibson and film mogul Harvey Weinstein, as well as singer Britney Spears and actress Lindsay Lohan.Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel said in a statement that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence". "We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said. Los Angeles County's top prosecutor, Nathan Hochman, said outside the courtroom on Monday that his office was "ready to proceed" with its case against Burke. He also acknowledged that the singer's change in lawyers could delay proceedings, require additional time to review the evidence, or result in the filing of a motion to dismiss the case. His team was ready for "zealous representation" by the defence, he said. Burke had already entered a not guilty plea to charges of first-degree murder, mutilation of human remains and child sexual abuse. He returned to court on Monday to have the charges against him formally read and re-entered the plea.The murder charges include special circumstances linked to financial gain that could make Burke potentially liable for the death sentence.Prosecutors allege Burke killed Hernandez because the teen had threatened to reveal his relationship with a minor and destroy his multi-million dollar music career.Evidence read in Los Angeles court during the preliminary hearing showed threats she made against him on 22 April 2025, stemming from arguments about his friendship with another girl."I swear to GOD I will kill u," one expletive-laden text from Hernandez read, followed by a threat to strangle him and tell her dad lies about him. "i will end ur career and ur life I will damage anything," the text went on.The following day, Hernandez went to Burke's Hollywood home in an Uber he had sent to pick her up.Prosecutors alleged that Burke stabbed her once she arrived.

schema.headline: US singer D4vd's celebrity lawyers withdraw from murder case

title: Sexual assaults in Ceuta happening almost every day, prosecutors say
description: Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Sp
body: Spanish prosecutors say 23 sexual assaults, including nine against children, have been recorded in Ceuta since the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave  at the end of July.That number meant there was almost one case every day, Ceuta's chief prosecutor Silvia Rojas said.She told El País newspaper migrant girls were "particularly vulnerable because of their irregular status in the territory".At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July and although most have returned, as many as 5,000 remain - leading to unrest in the autonomous city in North Africa and a crisis for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.Between 1,400 and 1,600 of the estimated 5,000 migrants still in Ceuta are children, according to Rojas.Among the suspected attackers are four Moroccans, three Spaniards and a Belgian, Efe news agency reports.There have been scenes of violence in recent days as tensions flare up between migrants and local residents. Sánchez called the second meeting of his national security council in a week on Tuesday to tackle the issue.Rojas said the influx had led to an exponential increase in sexual assault, and many victims did not file a report, either out of fear of because of their "current situation in Ceuta". The Spanish Society of Epidemiology said the border crisis had highlighted the difficulty in detecting and tackling violence against migrant women and girls.One 24-year-old woman from Morocco told the BBC she had "put her life in danger" by travelling to Ceuta, and described being sexually assaulted while sleeping among a group of men and women. "I was shocked… If I had known this, I wouldn't have come."Emergency doctor Susana Ascaso said last month her department at Ceuta University Hospital had treated several sexual assault victims, including one who was just 10 years old.Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said a multi-million euro aid package had been approved by the cabinet that would help provide essential services and cover care for unaccompanied children.The territory's conservative mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas, has called on Spaniards to take part in demonstrations across mainland Spain in support of Ceuta on Wednesday, which coincides with the city's annual holiday.The Spanish government is facing bitter criticism from its opponents for its handling of the crisis. The hard-right Vox party said Sánchez had not "lost control of Ceuta - he has handed it over".Arantxa Campos, president of the Ceuta Employers' Confederation, told the BBC: "We can't do anything unless these people leave. "We don't have a plan from the government. We don't have anything. We don't even know when they're going to finish screening everyone."The prime minister said on Monday that King Felipe VI would visit Ceuta "as soon as conditions allow", seen as an attempt to assert Spanish authority over the exclave. Morocco has a long-standing claim over Ceuta and its fellow autonomous city of Melilla. The last time a Spanish head of state visited the territories in 2007, Rabat pulled its ambassador from Madrid, and another royal visit may cause further diplomatic tensions.In an interview with Spanish radio channel Cadena Ser, Sánchez made a point of saying the king had not visited Ceuta for 20 years - even though Felipe has only been on the throne for 12 years and it was Juan Carlos who visited in 2007. He also asserted he was the only prime minister to have made an official visit to Ceuta while in office, having travelled there on 31 July as the crisis took hold. Some Spanish commentators noted that his remarks appeared to criticise the king, whom he then met later in the day.Unlike his political opponents, Sánchez has been careful to avoid blaming Morocco for stoking the surge of migrants. He said on Monday that no intelligence reports pointed to "any involvement in one way or another" from the Moroccan authorities.Instead he focused on disinformation on social media "associated with both Russia and Israel and an international far-right movement that always uses migration, not only to attack Spain but also Europe". He told Cadena Ser it did not mean "it must come from a state actor" and appeared to indicate the crisis had been stoked after the influx. Government spokeswoman Elma Saiz later confirmed his allegation, saying there was evidence that "various digital forums amplified what happened with the intention of fracturing and polarising Europe".Russia and Israel have both denied any involvement. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar accused the Spanish prime minister of "a blatant lie" and Russia's foreign ministry spokeswoman demanded proof to support Sánchez's allegations.A large number of social media posts appeared in August portraying the border fence between Morocco and Ceuta as safe and easy, even though at least 100 people died while trying to swim around the border fence, according to figures from the mayor.Spanish fact-checking website Maldita said before 30 July, when the influx began, messages circulated on Moroccan social media encouraging people to attempt the crossing, after a June ruling by Spain's Supreme Court.The opposition People's Party (PP) has criticised Sánchez for "exonerating" Morocco and pointing the finger in other directions. Borja Sémper, a spokesperson for the party, said tens of thousands of people could not have moved towards the Ceuta border without Morocco's knowledge.Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing.

schema.headline: Sexual assaults in Ceuta happening almost every day, prosecutors say

title: Russian attack hits rail workers in new deadly strikes on Kyiv
description: "Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said at a security
body: "Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said at a security summit in Kyrgyzstan.Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Overnight in Kyiv, eight people were killed and fires were reported in three city districts. Another four people were killed in the nearby town of Boryspil where a residential building was hit.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday morning that nearly 350 rescue workers had been working through the night in Kyiv and the surrounding region after the latest strikes.In a post on social media, he said Russia had fired a "significant number of jet drones and ballistic missiles". The strikes mark the sixth day of sustained Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv, in what appears to be a strategy aimed at exhausting Ukrainian air defences and undermining civilian morale.Russia's military warned over the weekend that its forces were preparing to carry out "massive" strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities.Eight other Ukrainian regions were attacked, Zelensky said, adding that an Indian national was among the casualties.Ukraine's Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivsky later said the Indian man - who turned 26 on Tuesday - was killed in Boryspil. The overnight attacks come after 38 people were killed in Russian strikes on a weapons depot in the Kyiv region on Friday, causing shells, mines and drones to detonate.Separately, a drone attack hit a major Russian Baltic Sea port in Ust-Luga, triggering a fire, Leningrad regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.Ukraine says targets like Ust-Luga - which handles millions of tons of petroleum products each year - are legitimate as they help finance Moscow's war effort.

schema.headline: Russian attack hits rail workers in new deadly strikes on Kyiv

title: Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema sworn in for second term while opponent detained
description: European Union observers said staff in many tallying centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced and cited weak veri
body: European Union observers said staff in many tallying centres did not record results on tally sheets as soon as they were announced and cited weak verification between digital entries and paper records.It added that returning officers frequently paused proceedings while awaiting instructions from headquarters.The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of opposition politicians.The authorities accused the opposition of planning an armed insurrection, which they denied.Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, had gone into hiding. They were detained by police last week and charged at the weekend.During his inauguration speech on Tuesday, Hichilema did not comment on his opponent's detention but said that the "pursuit of political power must never come at the expense of peace, security and stability in our country"."Democracy does not require us to agree on everything. It requires us to respect one another even when we disagree," Hichilema added. He also invited the opposition to work with his government for the good of the country: "When you have a good idea, we will listen to you."He was sworn into office amid jubilant scenes, as thousands of supporters gathered to celebrate the inauguration. His running mate Mutale Nalumango was also sworn in as vice-president.Presidents from Kenya, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Namibia and Tanzania were among several African leaders attending the inauguration ceremony at the National Heroes Stadium in the capital.When Hichilema, 64, came into office in 2021 after a landslide victory, the copper-rich nation had recently defaulted on its international debt and had an annual inflation rate of more than 24%."We inherited a broken-down country… the economy was declining," Hichilema told the BBC in Lusaka before the election.The former businessman negotiated a restructuring of the debt and rebuilt relations with foreign creditors. Inflation has also come down, but prices are still rising and many continue to struggle with the cost of living.Hichilema now wants to build on the foundations he said he laid over the past five years."We are moving from stabilisation to growth," the president said in his inauguration in speech. "Having done the heavy lifting in our first term, the next five years is all about growth and prosperity for all our people. I will continue to be a servant president for all the people of Zambia," he added. With a recent rise in the price of copper - which the World Bank says accounts for about 15% of GDP and more than 70% of exports - investors remain confident and appear ready to overlook post-election issues, the Bloomberg news agency reports.

schema.headline: Zambia's President Hakainde Hichilema sworn in for second term while opponent detained

title: John Galliano exhibition at New York's Met cancelled after backlash
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, John Galliano said he realised "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some"ByIan YoungsCulture
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, John Galliano said he realised "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some"ByIan YoungsCulture reporterJohn Galliano has cancelled an upcoming major exhibition celebrating his work as a fashion designer after it prompted criticism due to his previous conviction for making antisemitic remarks.The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York had announced an exhibition titled John Galliano: Horizons that was due to open in May 2027.But Galliano said on Monday: "After much reflection and discussion with the Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time."The British designer was sacked as creative director of Dior in 2011 and found guilty of abusing a Jewish curator in a restaurant in Paris.A court also heard that he hurled racist insults at her friend, who is of South Asian origin, and in a separate incident declared a love for Hitler.'I remain deeply sorry'At the time, he apologised for his behaviour and his lawyer blamed it on "work-related stress and multiple addictions".Galliano said in his statement on Monday: "I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it."I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture."It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one's conduct over time."Galliano added that he did not want "to distract from the remarkable work" of the Met's Costume Institute and said he recognised and respected that "an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some".Galliano's new statement noted his "15 years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Anna Wintour, pictured with Galliano in January, said he retained her "full support"As well as being the focus of the exhibition, Galliano and his work in fashion would have provided the theme for the next Met Gala.The star-studded event is due to take place on 3 May, coinciding with Yom HaShoah (Holocaust and Heroism Remembrance Day).Vogue global editorial director Anna Wintour, a trustee of the Met and co-chair of the Met Gala, gave her support to Galliano on Monday."John's decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is," she said."I believe this is the right decision, and both he and the Museum have my full support."'Misguided'Others had previously voiced their opposition to the Met's plan to commemorate Galliano.Julie Menin, speaker of New York City Council, said, external: "After my numerous and lengthy meetings and conversations with the Met, I am pleased that they have agreed to not honour John Galliano."From the beginning, I have told them that I strongly disagreed with this decision, and at this rising time of antisemitism, it had served as a gut punch to the Jewish community."This is the correct decision, as the harm and pain this was causing was simply unacceptable."Meanwhile, Jonathan Greenblatt, chief executive of the Anti-Defamation League, which aims to counter antisemitism, said that with antisemitism at "crisis levels", honouring Galliano would be "misguided"."Even Galliano ultimately recognised what the Met should have done from the start," he added. "This was the wrong move at the wrong moment. Timing matters."Galliano is regarded by some as one of the greatest fashion designers and returned to the fashion industry following his conviction, serving as creative director of Margiela for a decade until 2024.

schema.headline: John Galliano exhibition at New York's Met cancelled after backlash

title: Uniqlo, Muji: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen
description: India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment t
body: India's commerce minister Piyush Goyal led the country's largest-ever business delegation to Japan last week in a bid to expand trade and investment ties between the two countries. His visit came as Japan's deepening push into Asia's third largest economy has become increasingly more apparent. If you visit a shopping mall or a high street in Mumbai, Delhi or Bengaluru, it's hard to miss the growing number of Japanese consumer brands that have set up shop across India. Apparel giants Uniqlo and Muji and premium sneakers company Onitsuka Tiger have been around for a while, but are rapidly expanding.Niche players are also here - Nitori, a Japanese furniture maker, entered the market recently, while convenience store chain Lawson, external is on its way, with a plan to reportedly open 10,000 stores by 2050 in India, starting with Mumbai.It's not just retail. At a time when foreign lenders have been exiting their Indian bank portfolios, Japanese banks are aggressively bidding for Indian financial assets.MUFG Bank - Japan's largest bank - closed a deal to buy 20% of Indian shadow lender Shriram Finance for $4.4bn last year in what was the biggest ever foreign investment in India's financial sector.Last year also saw Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) becoming the largest shareholder in India's Yes Bank with a 24.22% stake.Japan Inc is now the largest contributor to India's booming ecosystem of global capability centres (GCCs) in the Asia Pacific.More than 100 Japanese firms operate these GCCs in the country, according to a recent Deloitte report, external. GCCs are offshore innovation hubs of multinationals that perform business critical functions such as R&D, corporate strategy and artificial intelligence development among a plethora of other key jobs."Japanese companies are having to look to India for growth. With the local population declining for the past 16-17 years there isn't just a slowdown in domestic demand, but a permanent shrinking of the market," Vipul Nath Jindal, Founder of Next Bharat Ventures, an impact fund backed by Suzuki Motor Corporation, which recently announced a $200m fund in India, told the BBC.At the same time, Japan's traditional markets for expansion have become increasingly less attractive, he says."Investment into China has fallen sharply amid geopolitical tensions and changing economic dynamics, the US market is more challenging because of tariffs and domestic competition, and the market size of other Southeast Asian economies is limited."Against this backdrop, India has become a natural target market for Japanese companies to drive long-term business growth.Economic ties between the countries gathered pace at a government-to-government level when they signed an agreement to liberalise trade nearly a decade-and-a-half ago.After Prime Minister Narendra Modi came to power in 2014, he elevated the relationship to a "special strategic and global partnership", setting a target of doubling the number of Japanese companies in India and launching marquee projects like India's first bullet train between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.But now, it is Japanese private firms that are driving business expansion in this latest investment up-cycle.At a landmark summit in July held during Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's first official visit to Delhi, Japanese companies announced $12.5bn in investments. They signed around 120 agreements in sectors ranging from semiconductors to green energy. In fact, Goyal has said Japan could prematurely meet its target of investing 10 trillion yen in the country. Beyond the large corporations, several Japanese small and medium-sized companies (SMEs) are also actively looking at tapping the Indian market, says Jindal.Hamamatsu City - where companies like Suzuki, Honda and Yamaha were founded and which has one of the highest concentrations of manufacturing SMEs in Japan - recently set up the Hamamatsu India Committee to explore how the city's small companies could expand into India.The rising interest in India has accompanied a fall in net Japanese investment in China which, as Toshiro Nishizaewa of the University of Tokyo wrote recently, external, is a reflection of "Japanese firms' autonomous market diversification strategies - a commercially driven reallocation of capital rather than a policymaker-led geopolitical shift from China to India".But Japanese firms aren't abandoning China en masse. What they are doing is "reducing concentration risk after several years of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical tensions", Shruti Pandalai, India Chair at the Sydney-based Lowy Institute think tank, told the BBC.India acts as a hedge against China-related risks, but there is also a growing overlap between Tokyo's economic security priorities and Delhi's manufacturing ambitions, which has strengthened the relationship despite significant political turnover in Tokyo, she says."With each successive government the targets have risen rather than fallen. That suggests the relationship has moved beyond leader-level diplomacy and become embedded in bureaucratic, corporate and strategic planning on both sides."For Delhi, which is starved of foreign investment, the Japanese money comes at a crucial time. India's burgeoning trade deficit with China has been a matter of grave concern and closer Japan-India cooperation could gradually reduce China's leverage in areas such as critical minerals and advanced manufacturing over the longer term, according to Pandalai.But challenges to expanding the full scope of this relationship are many, say experts."Japan remains deeply integrated into Chinese manufacturing networks, while India's engagement is more uneven but still significant in key sectors," writes Pratnashree Basu from the Observer Research Foundation for the online portal Scroll, external. "Economic interdependence, in this sense, constrains the scope for coordinated measures as these would impose significant commercial costs or provoke direct economic retaliation from China."Also, India remains a tough country to do business. Tax uncertainties, bureaucratic red tape, delays in land and environmental approvals are all long-documented challenges for foreign investors, including the Japanese.An ex-Japanese minister recently publicly blamed the government in Delhi for delays in the bullet train project, saying India kept "pushing its own self interest" and "flipping on promises" - criticism which the Indian government immediately rebuffed, external.Chinese state media, external was quick to pick up on the "rifts", using the incident as an example to highlight the gaps in India's ability to enforce contracts. It underscores why, even as it seals a raft of big-ticket economic and defence agreements, Delhi will need to work doubly hard to ensure Japanese investment momentum isn't disrupted - especially given its growing struggle to attract sustained foreign capital from elsewhere.Follow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: Uniqlo, Muji: Japan Inc is betting big on India as China risks deepen

title: The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts
description: The US and Canada appear no closer to resolving their ongoing trade dispute. Tensions have been simmering between the two neighbours since President D
body: The US and Canada appear no closer to resolving their ongoing trade dispute. Tensions have been simmering between the two neighbours since President Donald Trump returned to the White House just over 18 months ago, and unleashed a wide-ranging global programme of tariffs.Canada was one of the first countries the Trump administration hit with levies, and is one of two countries to respond with its own reciprocal measures.Currently, the US has hit Canada's key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles with tariffs, and last week imposed an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods.Canada has hit back with its own counter-tariffs on American goods, announcing on Tuesday what it calls a "dollar-for-dollar" and "strategic" retaliation designed to match the US tariffs.With no resolution in sight, how has this enduring trade war affected Canada and the US, and what could come next?Here are five charts to help break it all down. The US economy is much larger and the impact of Canada's counter-tariffs won't be as stark.But some states will feel the pain of Canada's retaliation more than others, with tariffs levied on C$28bn worth of US goods from steel to furniture, cosmetics and toilet paper, as of 8 September.According to data by Statistics Canada, the swing state of Ohio will be hardest hit, with C$3.2bn - or 12% - of its exports soon to be tariffed by Canada, followed by Illinois and Pennsylvania.For Ohio, it's the tax on steel that will particularly hurt, as well as the tax on laundry machines. In Illinois, where farm equipment giant John Deere is based, it will be the new tariffs on farm and construction equipment. Derek Holt, an economist with Scotiabank, noted that Canada's counter-tariffs appear to be "very deliberately oriented" towards some swing states that could decide the US balance of power in the upcoming midterm elections.Some businesses are adapting to find customers elsewhere. Matteo Sgaramella, who owns Toronto-based menswear clothing company Outclass, told the BBC he has started attending trunk shows in Paris instead of New York, helping him reach more customers in Europe."The reception has been amazing," he said, adding that some European stores are particularly enthused about supporting Canadian products due to the ongoing trade war with the US."We're kind of seen as the one country that's kind of standing up to the Americans right now," Sgaramella said.Other businesses, however, are struggling to diversify their trade, particularly in Ontario manufacturing sectors that are deeply integrated with the US.A recent report by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce pointed out three such regions in Ontario - Oshawa, London and Kitchener-Cambridge-Waterloo - as being particularly vulnerable."These cities remain heavily tied to the US market, while growth in exports outside the US has been limited or insufficient to offset broader weakness in trade activity and local economic conditions," the report said.While some businesses are lagging, foreign direct investment into Canada hit C$96.8 billion in 2025, the highest inflow of capital to the Canadian economy since 2007.Canada's economy also strongly rebounded in the second quarter of 2026 to 3.3% growth in the country's GDP, thanks to a jump in exports and domestic investment. These latest figures have warded off recession concerns, at least for now.Carney is hoping to attract even more investment. In September, his government will host the first-ever Canada Investment Summit, bringing major investors, CEOs and business leaders to Toronto for two days.

schema.headline: The US-Canada trade war in 5 charts

title: US Open 2026: Thea Frodin follows in Serena Williams' footsteps after playing idol in 'King Richard' film
description: Thea Frodin once played a young Serena Williams on the big screen. Now, the teenager is ready to follow in the American great's footsteps at the US Op
body: Thea Frodin once played a young Serena Williams on the big screen. Now, the teenager is ready to follow in the American great's footsteps at the US Open.Five years ago, Frodin was chosen as a tennis-playing body double for the actress cast as her childhood idol in the Oscar-nominated film 'King Richard'.That involved the then 12-year-old American working alongside actor Will Smith as he portrayed Richard Williams, the father of sisters Serena and Venus."Being able to play the role of somebody that I looked up to for my whole life was super special," Frodin told the WTA website., external"I was honoured. She was one of the players that I looked up to most, just when I was starting to play."She's such an inspiration to me."Now, Frodin will make her main-draw singles debut at her home Grand Slam, where Serena and Venus will this year team up in the doubles.To make the occasion even more special, she has been drawn against world number two Elena Rybakina, a two-time major winner and the reigning Australian Open champion."I'm trying to stay in the moment as much as possible," said Frodin. "This is a huge opportunity for me to enjoy the moment, have fun and see what I can do. "The atmosphere, how loud the crowd will be, I feel like I fit well in that environment."It has not taken long for Frodin to secure her maiden appearance at the sport's highest level.The 17-year-old earned a wildcard into this year's US Open women's singles competition - just as Venus Williams has done - by winning the United States Tennis Association' (USTA) Girls' 18s National Championships.It comes in a year where Frodin reached the semi-finals of the Australian Open girls' singles - her best result as a junior at a major.She also made her qualifying debut on the WTA Tour as a wildcard in Miami, and pushed former world number 35 Viktorija Golubic in a three-set loss in her first meeting with a player ranked inside the top-100.But on Tuesday, she will walk out for the biggest match of her life."To be standing here right now and actually getting a chance to play in the main draw, it means everything," said Frodin."[Rybakina] is number two for a reason, so I'm expecting a battle. Hopefully, I can bring out my best level against her."And, while she has never met the Williams sisters, Frodin is hoping that can change this fortnight."Hopefully, if I get a chance to hit with them or just meet them, anything, I'll take it," Frodin added."That would be incredible. That would be a dream."

schema.headline: US Open 2026: Thea Frodin follows in Serena Williams' footsteps after playing idol in 'King Richard' film

title: Ukraine war: What to make of Modi's plea to Putin to end conflict
description: If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war
body: If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly? The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses. Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades.Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries. But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association.Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs.So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats. As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war.This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine.Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table.He didn't. And he hasn't.There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations.To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied:"Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path."Polite, but vague. And non-committal.After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long.And "moving forward" at what pace?And, crucially, on which path?All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success.Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on.Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory.And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country.

schema.headline: Ukraine war: What to make of Modi's plea to Putin to end conflict
